articles.title: Red Roses: England's Delaney Burns on key opportunity to progress international career
articles.summary: As Delaney Burns hopes to be selected to face Australia, she talks to BBC Sport about another opportunity to add to her six caps in a so-far whirlwind career.
articles.body:
Delaney Burns revealed to her England team-mates that at 15 years old she had a 'short back and sides' - it went down well.

Having been selected to speak at one of the Red Roses 'connection meetings', the 24-year-old admitted she had "never been so nervous to talk in front of a group of people" in her life.

But the second-row was a roaring success as she covered her rugby journey, life in Bristol and 'that' haircut.

As she prepares to face Australia this Saturday, she has another opportunity to add to her six caps in what has been a whirlwind career so far.

Still only 24, Burns won her first three caps for England in 2023, then had to patiently wait for a call-up into the 2026 Six Nations squad to add three more.

With Abbie Ward, Rosie Galligan and Zoe Stratford all away from the squad pregnant or on maternity leave, the upcoming WXV Global Series is a significant opportunity for Burns.

"This is the first kind of campaign that I've been brought in from the start," she says.

"Being deemed as a more experienced forward, especially around the line-out, is something I want to hold myself quite high to and we do have a few younger players in the squad now, a few people coming through. So, I'm just trying to be a bit more of a person of knowledge to look to and help them out and build on my own strength."

Having missed out on one of England's 32-contracted places , she's focusing on her defence this season and wants to reach the next level.

As Burns continues to find her feet in the squad, an area she's excelled in off-field has been her work with the Bristol Bears Foundation. She coaches and gives talks to girls at schools in the greater Bristol area, covering more than just rugby.

"We talk about the menstrual cycle and how it affects you," she says. "Rugby is a really good sport to help with the idea of body image.

"We look at the effects that social media has in terms of too much screen time and filtering and AI. How to stay mentally safe as well as physically safe.

"There's some really deprived areas of Bristol - our whole mantra is to take those areas and do what we can to give the kids in those communities an opportunity, which I find very rewarding."

The impact of the work she's done with the foundation has seen the launch of a South Bristol girls team that's attracted 50-60 players and counting.

As she seeks a seventh cap against Australia on Saturday, will she take any of her own advice?

"I should listen to my own voice a bit more, probably," she says. "There are times where I definitely find myself in a bit of a weird headspace, camp is always hard.

"It's really rewarding and it's an exciting place to be and I wouldn't change it for the world, but equally it can be quite difficult. So yeah, listening to my own advice probably would be quite beneficial."

One of Burns' greatest fans is her grandad. If selected on Saturday, he'll be making the trip up to Manchester from Poole.

"He got me into rugby, trained me and goes to all the games he can," she says.

The stories about old hairstyles may have raised a few smiles among team-mates, but Burns is taking a more serious approach to the season ahead.

If selected against Australia, she will have another opportunity to add to her international experience and strengthen her place in an increasingly competitive Red Roses squad, with one of her biggest supporters watching on from the stands.

Forwards: Sarah Bern (Bristol Bears, 84 caps), Hannah Botterman (Bristol Bears, 62 caps), Delaney Burns (Bristol Bears, 6 caps), Abi Burton (Trailfinders Women, 9 caps), May Campbell (Saracens, 5 caps), Mackenzie Carson (Gloucester-Hartpury, 29 caps), Kelsey Clifford (Saracens, 25 caps), Amy Cokayne (Sale Sharks, 94 caps), Maddie Feaunati (Exeter Chiefs, 27 caps), Bryony Field (Saracens, uncapped), Haidee Head (Trailfinders Women, 1 cap), Lilli Ives Campion (Loughborough Lightning, 8 caps), Hayley Jones (Trailfinders Women, uncapped), Sadia Kabeya, (Loughborough Lightning, 32 caps), Haineala Lutui (Loughborough Lightning, 4 caps), Alex Matthews (Gloucester-Hartpury, 82 caps), Sophie McQueen (Gloucester-Hartpury, uncapped), Maud Muir (Gloucester-Hartpury, 53 caps), Marlie Packer (Harlequins, 116 caps), Demelza Short (Bristol Bears, 4 caps), Morwenna Talling (Sale Sharks, 29 caps)

articles.title: Rob Baxter: Exeter boss says England should pick English-based players
articles.summary: Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says England's rules on selecting only home-based players are the right thing for the domestic game.
articles.body:
Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says England's rules on selecting only home-based players are the right thing for the domestic game.

Former England forward Courtney Lawes has called for overseas-based players to be eligible to be picked for the England side.

The 37-year-old, who has won 105 England caps, returned to the Prem this summer with Sale, having spent two years at French side Brive where he was ineligible to represent his country.

Under England's selection policy, players can only be called up from overseas clubs in exceptional circumstances.

Baxter feels it is important the rules are not changed.

"I just don't think, for the good of the English game, you can do it," he told BBC Sport. "It's not that I don't understand the arguments, I do.

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes

"There's two arguments here, do you just want to make all the best players available to play for England or do you want to build Premiership Rugby as part of how you build the England team?

"If the two go together then you have to have some kind of rules and regulations around where the English players play.

"I always caveat any argument and say selfishly I'm talking about what's good for Exeter Chiefs as well - because what's good for Exeter, and every other Premiership side, is knowing there's a real reason for your best English players to stay in this country.

"If it just comes down to purely finance, then it's a tough, competitive situation for us, and when people just throw it out there that players should be allowed to play anywhere they like, I think you've got to look down at the deeper repercussions of what may actually happen in the English game overall."

Under the rules as they stand, England are unable to call on players such as Toulouse back row Jack Willis - who was voted the best player in France in 2024-25 - as well as Kyle Sinckler, Manu Tuilagi, Billy Vunipola, Lewis Ludlam and former Exeter star Sam Simmonds.

Prem clubs benefit from central payments from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) for their England players, with the national side having a greater say on their management as a result.

England's policy is similar to that of Ireland and New Zealand, while nations such as Scotland, South Africa and Australia do pick players from overseas.

"You can't pick and choose a model just to decide this is what will be good or bad for a country," added Baxter.

"For some countries they're very strict on it and it works really well for them. We've got to decide what we're comfortable with and stick to it."

articles.title: Raffi Quirke: Scrum-half excited by Newcastle project
articles.summary: Raffi Quirke says leaving Sale Sharks was one of the hardest decisions he has had to make, but is impressed with how things are taking shape at a revamped Newcastle Red Bulls.
articles.body:
Scrum-half Raffi Quirke says that leaving Sale Sharks was one of the hardest decisions he has ever had to make, but has been impressed with how things are taking shape at a revamped Newcastle Red Bulls.

Quirke is one of 25 new arrivals at Kingston Park, with the Red Bull ownership looking to improve on a team which has finished bottom of the table for the past four seasons.

The move north means stepping away from his boyhood side and familiar surroundings, but the 25-year-old is excited by the challenge of pushing Newcastle forward in a new era for the club.

"It was probably one of the hardest decisions that I've ever had to make - having those conversations with people who gave me my first ever opportunity, leaving all my home mates, family, friends from school," Quirke told the Rugby Union Weekly podcast.

Kiwi Christie chosen as Newcastle captain

"It was a huge decision but I just felt as though I was at a point in my career where I needed to have a new chapter and get out of my comfort zone.

"It's been really cool - new team, new players, new coaches. The whole thing is an exciting new project. We are all getting aligned but it has been an exciting start.

"It feels massively new to me [changes at Newcastle] but even for the lads that have been here before - they have changed the changing rooms up, there are new coaches, they are holding players a lot more accountable in sessions and feedback. The fitness sessions have been harder, everything has been so much harder - they are all saying 'this is what we have needed'.

"Coming from Sale, Newcastle have been bottom of the league for quite a few years now, so I was expecting there to be lots of things that needed to be changed or picked up on, but I feel like it is already happening."

Being one of so many new additions at Newcastle does not come without its challenges, but Quirke is excited by the prospect of building relationships and a winning team practically from scratch.

"We need to try and get connected as quickly as possible, both on and off the pitch so we have that understanding," he said.

"I was at Sale since I was 15, growing up with players there. I knew everyone's habits, we knew everything about each other, whereas at Newcastle I know a few people from Sale but I'm trying to get to understand everyone else.

"People have come from New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland, all over. People have been playing in France - everyone's culture is so different so it is about trying to get honed in on the same goal, understanding each other and what makes everyone tick. It has been really exciting.

"We had a trip to Austria which was really good to spend lots of time together because no-one is going back home to their wives and families. We had a couple of good socials.

"We've also had a couple of good socials just on weekends to spend time together off the pitch. It seems like a group that is really sociable anyway. If you went for dinner with the team, you wouldn't mind what table you were sat at.

"If you were to join a team that is already established there are cliques, whereas we are all joining here. If there is an initiation the whole team will be doing it!"

Quirke is also keen to use the move to help him work his way back into the England setup on a consistent basis.

"Speaking to the coaches and people higher up, they really wanted me to be back playing for England and pushing me to my limits - and that is what I really wanted to hear," he said.

"I've had ups and downs in terms of selection and injuries at really crucial times, which has been really frustrating. Hopefully this move really sparks a new start. I want to be playing for England again - that's my main goal."

articles.title: 'Almost non-existent' - Shane Williams on WRU schools support
articles.summary: Former Wales and Lions wing Shane Williams says pathways support for schools and colleges from the Welsh Rugby Union is "almost non-existent".
articles.body:
Former Wales and British and Irish Lions wing Shane Williams says financial support for schools and colleges rugby from the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) is "almost non-existent".

Wales' record try scorer is head of rugby at Ysgol Dyffryn Aman and suggests that support is reserved for elite players tied to regions.

The 49-year-old warns that good players are being lost because of a lack of WRU investment in student pathways.

"It's the most important part of it all," Williams told Radio Wales Breakfast.

"Where do these youngsters come from? Are we looking after them in the pathway?

"Are we just prioritising the elite players that the regions are looking after? And the answer to that is 'yes'.

"We need far more help and we try and do our best as head of rugby and coaches in these schools and colleges, but we don't seem to be getting much back at the minute.

"It is frustrating, I see a lot of good players coming through the system and I see a lot of good players being lost in the system or lost to England at the minute."

Last month, former Wales captain Jonathan Davies called for the WRU board to step down.

Businesswoman Hayley Parsons had already called for them to stand down before Davies did the same, while former Principality Building Society chief operating officer Rob Regan has offered to oversee an interim board.

In a statement, the WRU board did not directly address the calls for its members to resign but stated "the kinds of personal insults and attacks that have become far too commonplace are unacceptable".

The board also doubled down on its commitment to cut the number of professional teams from four to three by 2028, with WRU-owned Cardiff and privately-backed Dragons set to be given licences.

That announcement has plunged the futures of Scarlets and Ospreys into doubt, with the west licence either being awarded to the Llanelli-based side or their Swansea-based rivals.

Asked whether he still had faith in those running the game in Wales, Williams, who coaches in west Wales, said: "No, I don't have much faith, to be honest with you."

"I think they just took a little break in deciding what was going to happen, but knowing deep down in their hearts that they wanted it to be three regions.

"We as coaches know the uncertainty of who's going to remain as a region next year and that is very difficult.

"But what we are trying to do and what we do need is a bit more support in the pathway side of the rugby.

"We talk about the regions, we talk about the national team, but where do they think these players come from?

"I can answer that for you straight away. That is schools and colleges."

In its response the WRU stated: "The schools game in Wales is an integral part of our future strategy and we already provide significant funding and support in this area.

"After restructuring our community rugby department in 2025 we are now able to provide dedicated support to all clubs and schools throughout the country.

"We fund and run a number of competitions for schools including those which culminate in National Finals days held at either Principality Stadium or Rodney Parade each year."

images.caption: Image caption, Former wing Shane Williams scored a record 58 tries in 87 games for Wales between 2000 and 2011

articles.title: England rugby squad: Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant told to ‘go above’ Gallagher Prem rivals to earn spot back
articles.summary: The England internationals have returned to the Gallagher Prem but were left out of Steve Borthwick’s side’s recent camp; Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant have five competitive fixtures to play themselves into the autumn squad
articles.body:
Steve Borthwick recently named his squad for his three-day camp that started on Sunday, with Lawes and Marchant left out despite their return to the Gallagher Prem with Sale Sharks making them eligible for selection.

It was understood the England head coach wanted to see how the pair, who had been playing for French clubs Brive and Stade Francais respectively, got on before handing them a spot back in the team.

Now, defence coach Richard Wigglesworth has confirmed they are waiting to see how the pair fare on their return to England's top flight.

"We want as much quality as we can have in the league but they are going to have to go and play well," Wigglesworth said when asked about centurion Lawes and useful midfield option Marchant.

"There are some good players in the room and to pick them you have to leave someone else out, so they would have to go over and above that I would say.

"It's great to have Courtney back. He has unbelievable experience, is an England legend and has been flying in pre-season, as everyone is.

"There is a real excitement about watching him back in the Prem, so I'm enjoying that.

"I have actually bumped into Joe Marchant walking around living quite close to me, so I caught up with him and it is great to have him back."

Rugby union rules state only players who compete in the Gallagher Prem can be selected, meaning both players have put themselves back into contention.

Lawes retired from international rugby after the 2023 World Cup, but his return to home soil has raised hopes that he could feature at the 2027 World Cup in Australia at the age of 38.

"Everyone's case is individual in where you want to play your rugby and what you want to do," Wigglesworth said. "I couldn't have given up the chance of England because I didn't play as much as loads of people.

"But Courtney has said 'I've got an itch here and I'm coming back'. How good is that as a statement? 'I am coming back because I want to do this'.

"That level of determination and the qualities he has should put himself in a good spot. Experience, he has certainly got that. We are keen to watch him play."

The Nations Championship begins on November 6, with England taking on Australia on November 8.

images.caption: Image: Back rower Courtney Lawes offers serious experience at international level
Image: Steve Borthwick is waiting to see how the two former internationals get on

articles.title: Steve Borthwick: England head coach set for contract extension past 2028 Six Nations
articles.summary: England head coach Steve Borthwick will have his contract extended past the 2028 Six Nations in a bid to avoid uncertainty over his future before and during next year's Rugby World Cup.
articles.body:
England head coach Steve Borthwick will have his contract extended past the 2028 Six Nations in a bid to avoid uncertainty over his future before and during next year's Rugby World Cup.

As it did with Red Roses boss John Mitchell before the 2025 World Cup, the Rugby Football Union has moved to ensure Borthwick and his staff have some clarity over their positions going into the global showpiece.

According to RFU performance director Conor O'Shea, extending Borthwick's deal into the middle of 2028 will allow time to decide who leads the team in the longer-term.

"You don't want them looking for a job going into [a World Cup]," O'Shea explained.

"Everyone knows it will be judged on the World Cup, but you can't have a group of coaches going in with that uncertainty, especially when you look at the timing.

"So we will give that certainty, and that will give us time to look properly."

Following a review into England's "horrendous" Six Nations earlier this year, Borthwick has been backed to lead the team through to the World Cup, with O'Shea adding he can't see a scenario where Borthwick isn't in charge in Australia.

In the July leg of the Nations Championship, England recovered from a bruising defeat by South Africa in Johannesburg to vanquish Fiji in Liverpool and edge out Argentina to finish the campaign with two wins from three.

However at this stage the RFU has stopped short of committing to Borthwick on a long-term basis, unlike Ireland, who have signed their head coach Andy Farrell up to 2031.

"I see in Steve someone who bleeds England, and wants England to succeed more than anything you can imagine," O'Shea said.

"This England team is unequivocally one of probably five teams who can win the World Cup next year. I believe this team can win a World Cup.

"If over this next 12 months this England team shows the best version of itself, I know it can beat anyone in the world."

Conor O'Shea: Borthwick's contract, overseas rule & Red Roses

Selection rules 'best for English rugby'

As was the case for a number of his predecessors, Borthwick is only able to select players based in the English Prem, meaning the likes of Toulouse flanker Jack Willis – one of the outstanding performers in the French Top 14 – is ineligible for his country.

Cap centurion Courtney Lawes, who has returned to English rugby with Sale after two seasons at Brive, believes the RFU should review the policy to ensure the best players are available.

But O'Shea is adamant the ruling is what works for English rugby as a whole, and has warned against the impact of loosening the policy.

"It is something done not just for England, but for English rugby," O'Shea said.

"As of now, if all the best players were picked by England and went abroad, and we had less of the top players in our league, the unintended consequence towards investment into that from some of our owners… why would you invest in the pathways if the best players are going to be taken away?

"I get it completely, the life experiences are great. But for the English game, it is absolutely the right thing."

England should pick English-based players - Baxter

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes

Since joining the RFU in January 2020, O'Shea has overseen England women's global dominance, aided by the establishment and development of Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR).

And while the resources and player numbers at England dwarf those at many of their rivals, O'Shea rejects the notion that the Red Roses can ever be too strong.

The world champion Roses are unbeaten in four years and have won every Six Nations since 2018.

Conversely in the men's game, no nation has won three Six Nations in a row in the professional era.

"Does competitive tension create greater commercialisation and broadcast? I get all that," O'Shea said.

"But I do think when you look at the PWR, and what we have done in terms of allowing a lot of players to come over here and allow them the platform to develop as players, England plays a huge role in driving that.

"Was it bad when you had a dominant Tiger Woods, or Serena Williams? What about celebrating what they are. They have been the standard bearer."

Image caption, O'Shea (r) was previously head coach of Italy and director of rugby at Harlequins and London Irish

articles.title: Steve Borthwick: England head coach set for contract extension beyond 2028 Six Nations
articles.summary: Steve Borthwick is set to have his England contract extended beyond the 2028 Six Nations; the RFU will hand Borthwick the extension to avoid uncertainty around his future before and during next year's World Cup
articles.body:
The RFU will hand Borthwick the extension to avoid uncertainty around his future before and during next year's World Cup.

RFU performance director Conor O'Shea said: "You don't want them looking for a job going into [a World Cup].

"Everyone knows it will be judged on the World Cup, but you can't have a group of coaches going in with that uncertainty, especially when you look at the timing.

"So we will give that certainty, and that will give us time to look properly."

Borthwick has been back to lead England to the World Cup, following a "challenging" Six Nations review.

England came into the 2026 championship on an 11-Test winning run, but despite starting with victory over Wales they ended up suffering four defeats from five including away to Italy for the first time in history and a record home loss to Ireland.

The end result was Borthwick's side finishing fifth in the Six Nations standings just over 18 months before the next Rugby World Cup in Australia in 2027.

Last week, RFU CEO Bill Sweeney said Borthwick would be backed after a review into England's worst-ever Six Nations showing.

"This has been a thorough and honest review, and it is clear that improvement will come from addressing several areas rather than chasing one simple answer," Sweeney said.

"Steve has engaged in this process with full openness and has clear plans in place to address these findings. We are all behind him and his coaching team going into the Nations Championship and the series of matches leading into Rugby World Cup 2027."

Meanwhile, Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant must outshine their domestic rivals when the Gallagher Premiership season starts after being warned they will not walk straight back into England's autumn squad.

Defence coach Richard Wigglesworth has outlined what is required from the Sale duo in the five competitive fixtures that take place before Borthwick names his squad for the second phase of the Nations Championship.

Lawes and Marchant, members of the 2023 World Cup squad, have become available for England selection again after returning from spells at French clubs to join the Sharks over the summer.

Both players would be valuable assets for Borthwick, Test centurion Lawes providing experience, leadership and back-row pedigree while Marchant offers another option in the problematic midfield department.

England will closely monitor their progress over the coming weeks and for all their pedigree, they need to prove themselves again.

"We want as much quality as we can have in the league but they are going to have to go and play well," Wigglesworth said.

"There are some good players in the room and to pick them you have to leave someone else out, so they would have to go over and above that I would say.

"It's great to have Courtney back. He has unbelievable experience, is an England legend and has been flying in pre-season, as everyone is.

"There is a real excitement about watching him back in the Prem, so I'm enjoying that.

"I have actually bumped into Joe Marchant walking around living quite close to me, so I caught up with him and it is great to have him back."

Lawes announced his retirement after the last World Cup but his return to these shores has reignited his desire to add to his 105 caps, raising the possibility of his involvement in Australia 2027 as a 38-year-old.

Under Rugby Football Union rules, only players competing in the Prem can be selected by Borthwick and by returning from France he comes into consideration.

"Everyone's case is individual in where you want to play your rugby and what you want to do," Wigglesworth said. "I couldn't have given up the chance of England because I didn't play as much as loads of people.

"But Courtney has said 'I've got an itch here and I'm coming back'. How good is that as a statement? 'I am coming back because I want to do this'.

"That level of determination and the qualities he has should put himself in a good spot. Experience, he has certainly got that. We are keen to watch him play."

articles.title: Steve Borthwick: Contract bump falls short of vote of confidence
articles.summary: England head coach Steve Borthwick's extra six months buys time but doesn't indicate reserves of confidence from his Rugby Football Union employers.
articles.body:
"Horrendous" is not a word anyone wants to hear in their appraisal.

It was, however, the one chosen by Conor O'Shea, the man responsible for overseeing England's international success, to describe the men's team's 2026 Six Nations campaign.

And many fans will find it entirely apt.

England won only one match, their worst return since the tournament's expansion a quarter of a century ago. They lacked cohesion, discipline and tactical variety. It prompted profound, widespread questions about the future of head coach Steve Borthwick.

But, O'Shea revealed to Rugby Union Weekly, it has also preceded a contract extension for Borthwick.

Borthwick's terms now extend beyond the conclusion of the 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia to the end of the Six Nations the following year.

The contrast of O'Shea damning England's performances in one breath, while committing more time and money to the man in charge of them will be curious to many.

"You don't want the coaches looking for a job going into tournament," O'Shea explained.

"If they have no certainty, that is the worst case.

"So we'll give that certainty to the group, but then that will give us time to be able to look properly when it comes to the World Cup."

While New Zealand's swift renaissance under new coach Dave Rennie might give pause for thought, only the most disastrous dip in form would shake England determination to stick with Borthwick for that tournament in a year's time.

The extra six months added to Borthwick's deal beyond it is no fresh or significant vote of confidence though.

Nothing like the five-year extension that Ireland locked Andy Farrell into in June.

Rugby Union Weekly: Conor O'Shea on Borthwick's contract, overseas rule & Red Roses

RFU backs Borthwick but flags multiple Six Nations failings

The numbers behind Borthwick's nightmare Six Nations

The RFU has instead just expanded a holding pattern.

It hopes to dampen the speculation that would surround Borthwick if the end of his contract was tied to that of England's World Cup campaign. It has also bought some time for a decision after the tournament.

It was a tactic that worked with the Red Roses.

As they closed in on their own World Cup title in 2025, the possibility that either a shock defeat or the satisfaction of lifting the trophy would prompt coach John Mitchell to walk away was tempered by the fact his contract had been similarly extended.

In the wake of victory, the RFU was able to take its time and tie him down to another four years.

On this point, O'Shea interestingly revisited another home World Cup.

In 2015, England were humiliatingly knocked out of the pool stages of their own tournament.

But, amid the hand-wringing and reviews, O'Shea believes the RFU was bounced too quickly into jettisoning a coaching group, which was led by Stuart Lancaster and also contained Farrell, Graham Rowntree and Mike Catt.

Their exit paved the way for Eddie Jones and Borthwick, fresh from shocking South Africa with Japan at the same World Cup, to come in.

"Nobody had the gumption to say they are the right people," O'Shea recalls of the Lancaster-led group.

He contrasted the RFU's decision at the time with New Zealand's faith in a coaching ticket that suffered a shock exit from the 2007 Rugby World Cup, but went on to lift the next two titles.

If England go out early in next year's Rugby World Cup, it will be difficult to find anyone advocating for a further contract extension for Borthwick, who was appointed in December 2022.

Having been handed a peach of a draw, England are unlikely to cross paths with South Africa, New Zealand or France until a potential final.

The semi-finals, at least, is par for England. Anything less and Borthwick is unlikely to make the cut.

A winning percentage short of 60% over nearly four years in charge and only fleeting success in implementing a more ambitious, expansive gameplan leaves little goodwill to fall back on.

Back in March, RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney explained that succession planning continued to identify the next England head coach, as it did for all senior roles at the organisation.

Sweeney knows the end of a Rugby World Cup cycle, when moves are made and the coaching carousel hits full speed, is when those plans are most often tested.

Despite Borthwick's public contract bump, they will be continuing at pace and in parallel behind the scenes.

Image caption, Lancaster, Catt, Farrell and Rowntree (left to right) have gone on to have successful coaching careers elsewhere after they were sacked by England in 2015

articles.title: Ulster Rugby: Schmidt has an amazing eye for detail - Dermody
articles.summary: Ulster forwards coach Clarke Dermody praises Joe Schmidt's "amazing eye for detail" as he settles into his role at the Affidea Stadium.
articles.body:
Ulster forwards coach Clarke Dermody has praised Joe Schmidt's "amazing eye for detail" as he settles into his role at the Affidea Stadium.

Former New Zealand prop Dermody arrived from Super Rugby side Highlanders to replace Jimmy Duffy on Richie Murphy's coaching team.

Compatriot and former Ireland head coach Schmidt also arrived at the province this summer to take up the consultancy role of coach development adviser , following a spell as head coach with Australia.

While Schmidt's remit is the development of coaches across the province, Dermody says it is "awesome" to have him around the club as they prepare for the new season.

"A world-renowned coach with an amazing eye for detail," Dermody said of Schmidt when speaking to BBC Sport NI's Nicola McCarthy.

"He looks at the game differently to potentially everyone else. He's not the guy to push that on you, but if you're willing to ask, he's willing to give you that time and not say 'you must do it like this', but he has some ideas around the game.

"To have him around the club is awesome and I know it means a lot to the club for him to come in and spend time working with the youth and the pathways, but around enough for anyone else to rub shoulders with anyone who will want to."

Building blocks are for for Ulster to progress

Dermody joked that his main job is to "halve the scrum penalties" Ulster conceded last season, but is happy with what he has seen from the squad so far.

Ulster scored a narrow win over Edinburgh in a pre-season fixture last weekend and will host Ospreys on Friday [19:45 BST] in their final warm-up game before the United Rugby Championship [URC] begins at home to Edinburgh on 25 September.

Although Ulster had a disappointing finish to last season with defeat by Montpellier in the Challenge Cup final and a ninth-place finish in the URC seeing them miss out on the playoffs and a place in the Champions Cup, Dermody feels "the building blocks are there" to push on.

"While it was a tough end to the season, being able to put yourself in a final has to be commended," he added.

"I think there's enough excitement around that to kick-start the season.

"We aren't going to win every game, but there are a lot of games that were close enough to grab a few points that would have made the standing in the table at the end of the season different."

Dermody, who faced Ulster during his playing days with London Irish, recalls an "extremely hard team to beat" and feels getting it right in the forwards is crucial to compliment their attacking play.

"The style of play has changed a wee bit, but I think it would be remiss to overlook the need to express that physicality in the forwards," he continued.

"If you're in most games and the opposition walk off feeling that, you're in a good place."

images.caption: Image caption, Schmidt took up the role of consultancy role of coach development adviser at Ulster this summer
Image caption, Dermody took over from Jimmy Duffy as Ulster forwards coach this summer

articles.title: Dragons under pressure in URC after avoiding Welsh Rugby Union cut
articles.summary: Dragons set target of making the United Rugby Championship play-offs after avoiding being cut under Welsh Rugby Union plans.
articles.body:
Dragons chief executive Rhys Blumberg admits being saved from a Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) cut puts extra pressure on results - and has set an ambitious target of reaching the United Rugby Championship (URC) play-offs.

The governing body is pressing on with controversial plans to go from four professional men's clubs to three by 2028.

It was announced in July that privately-owned Dragons and WRU-owned Cardiff will be given licences, leaving Llanelli-based Scarlets and Swansea-based Ospreys competing to be the team in the west.

Asked at a meeting with supporters if the WRU's plans put more pressure on results, Blumberg replied: "Yes, I do, and I honestly think it will be a great year for us.

"If we do win more games then it's definitely not going to harm us as we go through this process with the WRU."

Wales lock Carter cleared for season start

Tuipulotu plays for Dragons - but will not be signed

Dragons are traditionally the worst performing of the Welsh quartet but made a big improvement in 2025-26.

Filo Tiatia's side made the semi-finals of the Challenge Cup and won three games and drew four times to claim 28 points in the URC, up from just nine points in a nightmare 2024-25 that featured a solitary victory.

They still finished one from bottom because of missed opportunities and were pipped to 14th by Scarlets on win count, meaning they have been Wales' lowest-ranked side in 18 of 23 seasons.

Dragons have not finished in the top half of the league since 2005 but Blumberg has set a lofty target of reaching the play-offs.

"We want the top eight, I have made that very well known to Filo and he is definitely on board with that as an ambition," he said.

"That would be a huge step up for us but last year we had the biggest swing in league points in the URC, so I am hoping to build on that.

"So, why not the play-offs? It's a really ambitious but realistic target."

Dragons will need a strong first block to achieve that objective with an opening fixture at Benetton on Friday, 25 September followed by home derbies against Scarlets and Ospreys.

Dragons will chase on-field progress in yet another season that will be played amid off-field uncertainty in Wales.

Blumberg admitted there was "an air of tension" between the professional clubs due to years of uncertainty and wrangling with the WRU.

Dragons are safe but still do not want a cut.

"We've consistently said that four teams should be a way forward. We stand by that," said Blumberg.

"Clearly, with the WRU now saying that three is the direction of travel, we'll be sitting on our hands for a minute, taking a deep breath on the basis that we've got some security for the first time in two and a half years."

The controversial proposals have led to calls for the governing body's board to resign and prompted legal action.

The WRU has said the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of the upcoming campaign.

Scarlets managing director Jon Daniels has insisted there are no plans for a merger with Ospreys and called for greater transparency from the WRU.

"It's not going to be straightforward, whatever they do. There are going to be legal battles," said Blumberg.

"However, if you are the chair or CEO of the Union and you've only got X amount of money – and that's a contentious point itself – and you are going to support three teams moving forward and one has to go, then at some stage you have got to make that happen.

"It has taken so long to get here, time that has been filled by so much nonsense and a lot of headaches.

"There has been no solution and no ending, and that continues. The WRU has said they are going to provide data as to why they are going to three.

"If that is the direction of travel – and it's not our preference – then we go ahead, organise the three-team agreement and move forward."

The WRU, who initially wanted to cut from four to two, insist finances make it impossible to field four competitive professional sides.

Blumberg said: "Are we making the most of every opportunity to maximise revenue? Are we managing all our costs as efficiently as possible?

"If that is being done and we are at a point where we can only afford X number of teams then the conversation is a really horrible one, but we need to have it."

It has been suggested in some quarters that Welsh rugby would thrive if it was to leave the URC and join the English league.

The existing 10-team Prem is set to expand to 12 clubs in 2029-30 with a desire to grow further.

"I have had no credible conversation or source that has told me there is a realistic prospect of Welsh clubs entering the English league in the foreseeable future," said Blumberg.

"Getting out of the URC, if that was something that the Union wanted to do, is not straightforward.

"I don't see an Anglo-Welsh league being credible in the foreseeable future, but I don't think there is any question that the appetite for that is generally there."

images.caption: Image caption, Dragons have finished in the bottom two in their last five seasons
Image caption, Rhys Blumberg joined Dragons as chief executive in 2024
Image caption, Dragons beat Newcastle in the Challenge Cup in 2025-26

articles.title: WXV Series: Clarke & Gallagher start for Scotland against Canada
articles.summary: Scrum-half Rhea Clarke will make her first start when Scotland begin their WXV Series campaign against Canada, while Evie Gallagher returns on the openside flank.
articles.body:
Scrum-half Rhea Clarke will make her first start when Scotland begin their WXV Series campaign against Canada in Edinburgh on Saturday.

Evie Gallagher returns on the openside flank for her first appearance since last year's World Cup.

She will partner captain Rachel Malcolm, who leads the team from the blindside, with Becky Boyd taking the number eight shirt for the match which will be broadcast live on BBC ALBA and BBC iPlayer (kick-off 16:10 BST).

Shona Campbell is selected on the left wing, joining the experienced pair of Rhona Lloyd and Chloe Rollie in the back three.

Glasgow fly-half Ceitidh Ainsworth and Exeter full-back Katie Buchanan, both uncapped, are among the replacements chosen by interim head coach Dave Butcher.

Second row Adelle Ferrie is also on the bench, having replaced the injured Alex Stewart in the squad.

World Cup runners-up Canada have won seven of their eight meetings with Scotland, including a 40-19 success in the group stage of the tournament last September.

After taking on Canada, Scotland have Tests against New Zealand and Australia.

Scotland: C Rollie, R Lloyd, R Phillips, M Smith, S Campbell, H Nelson, R Clarke; L Bartlett, L Skeldon, E Clarke, E Wassell, H Cunningham, R Malcolm, E Gallagher, B Boyd.

Replacements: A Sutcliffe, A young, M Poolman, E Donaldson, A Ferrie, C Ainsworth, H Ramsay, K Buchanan.

images.caption: Image caption, Rhea Clarke starts at scrum-half for Scotland at The Hive in Edinburgh

articles.title: England v Australia: Holly Aitchison included as Natasha Hunt makes comeback
articles.summary: Holly Aitchison will win her 50th England cap when she starts at fly-half in the Red Roses WXV opener against Australia on Saturday in Manchester.
articles.body:
Holly Aitchison will win her 50th England cap when she starts at fly-half in the Red Roses' WXV opener against Australia on Saturday in Manchester.

Aitchison, 28, started two of England's wins en route to their Six Nations Grand Slam earlier this year, but has been unable to supplant Zoe Harrison as head coach John Mitchell's pick at 10 for the biggest matches.

Aitchison is one of five changes to the England team that beat France in Bordeaux last time out.

Scrum-half Natasha Hunt makes her comeback from a knee ligament injury that has kept her out of action since the win over Ireland in April, while fellow World Cup winner Tatyana Heard makes her first Test appearance of the year after recovering from a foot injury.

May Campbell, whose five previous England appearances have come off the bench, makes her first Test start with resources stretched thin at hooker.

Amy Cokayne will miss the match through injury and Connie Powell is recovering from ankle surgery, while Lark Atkin-Davies is on maternity leave having had a daughter in June.

Their absences mean back-up hooker Bryony Field, who plays alongside Campbell at Saracens, is set to win her first senior England cap from the bench, where Hannah Botterman, who has not featured since 2025's World Cup final win, and Morwenna Talling are primed to make returns from injury.

Gloucester-Hartpury's Mia Venner, who finished joint top of last season's PWR try-scoring charts, come in on the wing.

Aitchinson, Heard and Talling all play for Sale Sharks, whose men's team host games at the CorpAcq Stadium, where Saturday's match takes place.

"I have very fond memories of the North West from my time with Sale Sharks so it's awesome to be able to take our game to this part of the country," said head coach John Mitchell, who spent two spells with the club as a player and a coach.

"Playing in a different part of the country allows us to be present in the community and keeps the game healthy. You've not only got to be visible, but if you can actually be close to your community, I think that's even better."

Unlike England's men, who are tied to Twickenham's Allianz Stadium by the commercial advantages of staging matches in an 82,000-capacity venue owned by the Rugby Football Union, the Red Roses are regularly on the road.

England will take on Canada for the first time since victory in the team's meeting in last year's Rugby World Cup final at Exeter's Sandy Park next weekend, before finishing the home leg of the WXV Global Series against New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on 26 September.

Away matches against Canada (twice) and the United States follow in October as part of the new-look event which aims to fill out the women's Test calendar away from the World Cup.

Australia have named the uncapped Amelia Whitaker on the wing. Whitaker, 20, is the niece of former Australia and Leinster scrum-half Chris Whitaker.

Elsewhere, exciting 19-year-old Caitlyn Halse, one of a clutch of Australians to have signed for Leicester for the next PWR season, is included at full-back.

England have won all eight of the teams' previous meetings, most recently prevailing 47-7 in the pool stages of last year's World Cup.

England: Kildunne; Venner, Jones, Heard, Moloney-MacDonald; Aitchison, Hunt; Carson, Campbell, Bern, Burns, Ives Campion, Burton, Kabeya, Feaunati

Replacements: Field, Botterman, Muir, Talling, Packer, Packer, Harrison, Rowland

Australia: Halse; Whitaker, Friedrichs, Moleka, Miller; Ellis, Wood; Hoy, Merlo, Pohiva, Leaney, Leonard, Tapsell, Bone, Palu Sekona

Replacements: Naden, Sikimeti, Karpani, Bemrose, Duck, Chancellor, Hinds, Smith

Live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, with live text coverage
